intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia-51 (SPG51) is caused by homozygous mutation in the AP4E1 gene (607244) on chromosome 15q21.2.

checks.claim: Autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia-51 (SPG51) is caused by homozygous mutation in the AP4E1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: In conclusion, we identified twins with autosomal recessive AP-4 deficiency associated with HSP and mycobacterial disease
checks.explanation: Paper reports homozygous AP4E1 nonsense mutation causing AR HSP; AP4E1 designated SPG51.

checks.claim: The AP4E1 gene is located on chromosome 15q21.2.
checks.evidence_quote: We identified a 139 kb (minimum) to 222 kb (maximum) homozygous deletion of chromosome 15q21.2 that includes the 5′ end of two genes: AP4E1
checks.explanation: The paper places AP4E1 within the deleted 15q21.2 region.

paragraphs.text: Autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia-51 (SPG51) is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder. Patients have microcephaly and infantile hypotonia that progresses to spastic paraplegia or spastic tetraplegia, severe intellectual disability, and absent or very limited speech. Most never walk independently. Other features include stereotypic laughter, drooling, lack of sphincter control, and, in some patients, seizures and cerebral and cerebellar atrophy. The disorder belongs to a group of conditions caused by deficiency of the adaptor protein complex-4 (AP-4).

checks.explanation: The paper describes a severe neurodevelopmental phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) reported 2 sibs, a woman (IV-4) aged 23 years and a man (IV-5) aged 22 years, from a consanguineous Palestinian-Jordanian family. The sister had microcephaly (-3 SD) and hypotonia at birth. By the first year of life, the hypotonia had progressed to spastic tetraplegia with hyperreflexia and generalized hypertonia. She never developed speech or independent walking. She had been wheelchair-bound since 5 years of age, which was also when generalized tonic-clonic seizures began. She had profound intellectual disability, drooling, stereotypic laughter, a Babinski sign, and lack of sphincter control. Her dysmorphic features included bitemporal narrowing, a long narrow face, a prominent pointed chin, downslanting palpebral fissures, a long nose with a wide nasal ridge, a short philtrum, a full everted upper vermilion, a prominent antihelix, and facial hypotonia. Brain MRI showed ventriculomegaly, cortical and cerebellar atrophy, reduced hippocampal volume, and diffuse white matter loss that was most pronounced in the frontal region and corpus callosum. EEG showed generalized theta slowing. Eye evaluation and hearing were normal.

paragraphs.text: Her brother, also reported by Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011), had microcephaly (-3 SD), neonatal hypotonia, and developmental delay. He acquired some dysarthric words but never normal speech. He walked with support, but increasing spasticity made him wheelchair-dependent by age 9 years. His seizures began as staring spells and became generalized tonic-clonic seizures at age 15. On examination at 22 years, he had spastic tetraplegia with hypertonia, hyperreflexia, and a Babinski sign. He also had outbursts of stereotypic laughter, drooling, jerky nystagmus, severe intellectual disability, and lack of sphincter control. Brain imaging showed moderate ventriculomegaly and prominent cisterns. Hearing was normal.

paragraphs.text: Abou Jamra et al. (2011) reported 8 affected individuals from 3 consanguineous families with mutations in AP4 subunit genes; 1 of the families carried an AP4E1 mutation. The patients had severe intellectual disability, absent speech, a shy character, stereotypic laughter, and muscular hypotonia that progressed to spastic paraplegia. Other features were microcephaly, foot deformity, decreased muscle mass of the lower limbs, inability to walk, and growth retardation.

paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2013) reported identical twin girls (P1 and P2), born to first-cousin Moroccan parents, who were 3 years old at last report. Both had intellectual disability, microcephaly (head circumference 46 cm (-2 SD) in P1 and 45.5 cm (-2.5 SD) in P2), and early infantile hypotonia. They developed spastic paraplegia of the lower extremities. Neither twin ever walked or spoke. Both had absent sphincter control, stereotypic laughter, drooling, short stature, and low body weight. They shared a discreet but remarkable facial gestalt with a prominent bulbous nose, a wide mouth, and coarse features. CT showed atrophy of the inferior vermis and cortical atrophy, and EEG showed diffuse slow waves. Both twins had astigmatism. P1 also had myopia and left-sided conductive hearing loss. Neither had seizures, hyperreflexia, a Babinski sign, or contractures. At 9 months of age, both developed unilaterally enlarged, inflamed axillary lymph nodes (BCG lymphadenitis). Lymphocyte subsets, immunoglobulins, complement, the IL-12/IFN-gamma circuit, and oxidative burst were all normal, and no immunologic abnormality was found to explain the mycobacterial disease. The authors proposed that the AP4E1 mutation was the most likely cause of the mycobacterial disease.

paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2018) restudied these Moroccan twin sisters at 8 years of age. They noted that the twins had hereditary spastic paraplegia due to the homozygous AP4E1 mutation and had suffered neonatal asphyxia at delivery. The twins also had Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, with BCG disease, enlarged inflamed axillary lymph nodes, and acid-fast bacilli on lymph node biopsy. Kong et al. (2018) attributed the mycobacterial disease to a homozygous SPPL2A mutation rather than to the AP4E1 mutation.

checks.explanation: The paper describes the Moroccan twins as eight years old at the time of study, supporting the age; however the paper does not frame this as a 'restudy' of previously reported patients, and the Methods note clinical evaluation at three years of age.

checks.explanation: Stated directly in the clinical description of P1 and P2.

paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2013) studied Moroccan identical twins, born to first-cousin parents, who had complex hereditary spastic paraplegia and BCG lymphadenitis. Using whole-exome sequencing, they identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in AP4E1 (R1105X; V5). The parents were heterozygous and a healthy sib was wildtype. The mutation was not found in 1,050 CEPH controls or 69 Moroccan controls. Patient EBV-B cells had normal levels of AP4E1 mRNA. However, AP-4-epsilon protein was barely detectable, and levels of AP-4-mu and AP-4-beta were also reduced. In patient fibroblasts and EBV-B cells, the amount of assembled AP-4 complex was more than 95% lower than in controls. The AP-4 binding partner tepsin was not detectable in patient fibroblasts.

checks.claim: The amount of assembled AP-4 complex in cells from the Moroccan twins with the AP4E1 R1105X mutation was more than 95% lower than in controls.
checks.evidence_quote: IMAGE J quantification indicated that AP-4 assembly levels were more than 95% lower than those of healthy controls

paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2018) restudied the same twins at 8 years of age. They attributed the twins' hereditary spastic paraplegia to the homozygous AP4E1 R1105X mutation and their mycobacterial disease to a coexisting homozygous SPPL2A splice site mutation.

checks.claim: Kong et al. (2018) restudied the Moroccan twins with the AP4E1 R1105X mutation at 8 years of age.
checks.evidence_quote: a family from Morocco including two affected eight-year-old monozygotic twin sisters (P1 and P2, Kindred A, Fig. 1a)
checks.explanation: Age of eight years and the AP4E1 R1105X genotype are both stated, but the paper does not present itself as a restudy of previously published patients.

checks.claim: Kong et al. (2018) attributed the Moroccan twins' hereditary spastic paraplegia to the homozygous AP4E1 R1105X mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: In addition to MSMD, the patients displayed hereditary spastic paraplegia due to a homozygous p.R1105X mutation of the AP4E1 gene.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Kong et al. (2018) attributed the Moroccan twins' mycobacterial disease to a coexisting homozygous SPPL2A splice site mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: Sanger sequencing confirmed that both P1 and P2 carried a homozygous c.733+1G>A mutation of the splice donor site of SPPL2A intron 6
checks.explanation: The twins carry a coexisting homozygous SPPL2A essential splice-site mutation, which the paper identifies as the cause of their MSMD.
